english: Ga is a tonal language; changes in the meaning of words may be brought about by tonal differences
Ga has seven vowels: a, e, ɛ, i, o, ɔ, u. Each vowel can be lengthened or shortened for speech and inflexion, but each retains a regular and constant value
ga: a e ɛ i o ɔ u

english: The long forms of the seven Ga vowels are: aa, ee, ɛɛ, ii, oo, ɔɔ, uu. The short and long forms should not be likened to the so-called closed and opened vowels in English
ga: aa ee ɛɛ ii oo ɔɔ uu

english: Short vowel 'a' sounds like the 'a' in English 'father', as in the Ga word for 'to come'
Short vowel 'e' sounds like the 'a' in English 'cake', as in the Ga word for 'to know'
Short vowel 'ɛ' sounds like the 'e' in English 'bet', as in the Ga word for 'to burst'
Short vowel 'i' sounds like the 'ea' in English 'read', as in the Ga word for 'child'
Short vowel 'o' sounds like the 'o' in English 'pole', as in the Ga word for 'to weep'
Short vowel 'ɔ' sounds like the 'o' in English 'pot', as in the Ga word for 'bottle'
Short vowel 'u' sounds like the 'oo' in English 'good', as in the Ga word for 'to jump'
Long vowel 'aa' sounds like the 'a' in English 'far', as in the Ga word for 'river'
Long vowel 'ee' sounds like the 'ay' in English 'lay', as in the Ga word for 'did'
Long vowel 'ɛɛ' sounds like the 'ai' in English 'fair', as in the Ga word for 'upbringing'
Long vowel 'ii' sounds like the 'ee' in English 'fee', as in the Ga word for 'children'
Long vowel 'oo' sounds like the 'o' in English 'so', as in the Ga word for 'fish'
Long vowel 'ɔɔ' sounds like the 'o' in English 'or', as in the Ga word for 'sleeping'
Long vowel 'uu' sounds like the 'wo' in English 'two', as in the Ga word for 'tent'
Ga consonants are the same as in English, except that c, q and x are not used
ga: b d f g h j k l m n ŋ p r s t v w y z

english: Digraph 'gb' as in the Ga word for 'to tear'
Digraph 'gw' as in the Ga word for 'sheep'
Digraph 'hw' as in the Ga word for 'to shake'; close to the 'wh' in English 'what'
Digraph 'jw' as in the Ga word for 'rubbish'
Digraph 'kp' as in the Ga word for 'to chew'
Digraph 'kw' as in the Ga word for 'to look'; close to the 'qu' in English 'quad'
Digraph 'ny' as in the Ga word for 'you (plural)'; close to the 'ny' in English 'canyon'
Digraph 'ŋm' as in the Ga word for 'palm fruit'
Digraph 'ŋw' as in the Ga word for 'the sky'
Digraph 'sh' as in the Ga word for 'to knock'; like the 'sh' in English 'she'
Digraph 'ts' as in the Ga word for 'to pluck'; close to the 'ch' in English 'church'
Trigraph 'shw' as in the Ga word for 'to blame'
Trigraph 'tsw' as in the Ga word for 'to strike'
It is difficult to get exact English sound equivalents for Ga digraphs and trigraphs; the examples given are only close approximations
ga: gb gw hw jw kp kw ny ŋm ŋw sh ts shw tsw

english: The Ga alphabet (uppercase) has 26 letters, including Ɛ, Ŋ and Ɔ; c, q and x are not used
ga: Niŋmaa Okadii: A B D E Ɛ F G H I J K L M N Ŋ O Ɔ P R S T U V W Y Z

ga: a b d e ɛ f g h i j k l m n ŋ o ɔ p r s t u v w y z
